lessons.title: Test Automation - 1
lessons.lesson_objective: *Demonstrate all supported slide types including multiple choice and feedback by choice configurations.

slides.slide_name: Introduction to Automation Concepts
slides.content:
What Is Automation?

Automation is the use of technology to perform tasks that would otherwise require manual effort. In a business context, automation reduces the time spent on repetitive work, minimizes human error, and allows teams to focus on higher-value activities.

There are two primary categories of automation relevant to this course:

  • Process automation — sequences of steps executed by a system without manual intervention
  • Content automation — the structured generation or population of content from a defined data source

Both categories share a common requirement: the underlying data must be accurate, complete, and consistently structured before automation can produce reliable results.

slides.slide_name: Multiple Choice — Question Feedback (Standard)
slides.question_body: Which of the following best describes the primary benefit of process automation in a business environment?

options.label: A
options.text: It eliminates the need for human oversight once deployed

options.label: B
options.text: It reduces time spent on repetitive tasks and minimizes manual error

options.label: C
options.text: It replaces all decision-making with system-generated outputs

options.label: D
options.text: It guarantees that all outputs are accurate without validation

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. Automation reduces manual effort and error on repetitive tasks, but it still requires human oversight and validation to ensure outputs meet quality standards.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Automation supports human work — it does not replace oversight. Focus on what automation reduces rather than what it eliminates entirely.

slides.slide_name: Multiple Choice — Feedback by Choice
slides.question_body: A team wants to automate a content import process. Which condition must be true before automation can produce reliable results?

options.label: A
options.text: The team must have a developer on staff to maintain the automation
options.feedback: Developer involvement is helpful but not the primary requirement for reliable automation output. The data itself must be correctly structured first.

options.label: B
options.text: The underlying data must be accurate, complete, and consistently structured
options.feedback: Correct. Automation amplifies whatever is in the source data. If the data is clean and consistently structured, the output will be reliable.

options.label: C
options.text: The automation must be tested in a production environment first
options.feedback: Testing in production introduces risk. The correct approach is to validate data quality and test in a safe environment before running against production systems.

options.label: D
options.text: All manual processes must be eliminated before automation is introduced
options.feedback: Automation and manual processes can coexist. Eliminating all manual steps is not a prerequisite — in fact, some steps benefit from remaining manual.

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. Clean, consistently structured data is the foundation of reliable automation.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the conditions required before automation can produce reliable results.

slides.slide_name: True or False — Standard Labels, Question Feedback
slides.question_body: Identify whether each statement about automation is True or False.

options.label: A
options.text: Automation can reduce the time spent on repetitive manual tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Once deployed, an automated process requires no ongoing human oversight.

options.label: C
options.text: Data quality directly affects the reliability of automation outputs.

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. Automation reduces effort on repetitive tasks and depends on clean data, but it still requires human oversight to remain reliable.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the core principles of automation. Focus on what automation improves versus what it cannot replace.

slides.slide_name: True or False — Feedback by Choice
slides.question_body: Read each statement and select whether it Applies or Does Not Apply to content automation best practices.

options.label: A
options.text: Source data should be validated before an automated import is run.
options.feedback: Correct. Validating source data before running automation prevents errors from being propagated at scale across all outputs.

options.label: B
options.text: Automation outputs should be accepted as final without spot-checking.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Spot-checking automation outputs is a best practice. Automation can introduce systematic errors that only become visible through manual review.

options.label: C
options.text: A failed automation run should be logged with enough detail to diagnose the cause.
options.feedback: Correct. Detailed failure logging is essential for diagnosing and resolving automation issues quickly and accurately.

slides.correct_feedback: Well done. You correctly identified all three best practices.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review automation best practices and consider what happens when errors go undetected at each stage.

slides.slide_name: Matching — Core Automation Terms
slides.question_body: Match each automation term to its correct definition.

options.label: A
options.text: Process automation
options.match: Executing a sequence of steps by a system without manual intervention

options.label: B
options.text: Content automation
options.match: Generating or populating content from a structured data source

options.label: C
options.text: Validation
options.match: Confirming that outputs meet expected standards before use

options.label: D
options.text: Run log
options.match: A persistent record of each step completed during an automated run

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You matched all four automation terms to their definitions accurately.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review each definition carefully. Focus on what each term describes in the context of an automated workflow.

slides.slide_name: Sort — Automation Phases
slides.question_body: Sort each activity into the correct phase of an automation workflow.

items.label: A
items.text: Validate source data for accuracy and completeness

items.label: B
items.text: Confirm all required fields are present in the input file

items.label: C
items.text: Test the automation against a small sample dataset

items.label: D
items.text: Spot-check a sample of outputs for accuracy

items.label: E
items.text: Archive the run log for audit and reference

items.label: F
items.text: Review failure screenshots to diagnose any errors

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You sorted every activity into the right phase of the automation workflow.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Think about whether each activity is a preparation step or a review step.

lessons.title: Test Automation - 2
lessons.lesson_objective: *Apply data quality principles across multiple slide types including feedback by choice configurations.

slides.slide_name: The Role of Data Quality in Automation
slides.content:
Why Data Quality Determines Automation Success

Automation amplifies whatever is in the source data. A process that runs correctly against clean data will produce reliable results at scale. The same process run against inaccurate or incomplete data will produce unreliable results at scale — and do so faster than any manual process could.

The four dimensions of data quality that matter most for automation are:

  1. Accuracy — Is the data correct and free from errors?
  2. Completeness — Are all required fields and values present?
  3. Consistency — Does the data follow the same format and conventions throughout?
  4. Timeliness — Is the data current enough to produce valid outputs?

Each dimension can fail independently. A dataset can be accurate but incomplete, or consistent but outdated. Reliable automation requires all four to be maintained together.

slides.slide_name: Multiple Choice — Data Quality Standard Feedback
slides.question_body: A content import automation run produces incorrect outputs across every lesson in a course. The automation logic ran without errors. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The automation tool has a software defect

options.label: B
options.text: The source data contained errors that were propagated at scale

options.label: C
options.text: The output format is incompatible with the destination system

options.label: D
options.text: The run log was not written during the process

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. When automation logic runs without errors but outputs are wrong, the problem is almost always in the source data. Automation propagates errors at the same scale as correct data.
slides.incorrect_feedback: When automation logic completes without errors, focus on the input rather than the tool. Errors in source data are the most common cause of systematic output failures.

slides.slide_name: Multiple Choice — Data Dimensions Feedback by Choice
slides.question_body: Which data quality dimension is most directly affected when a required field is missing from a record in an automation input file?

options.label: A
options.text: Accuracy
options.feedback: Accuracy refers to whether the data values are correct, not whether fields are present. A missing field is a completeness issue rather than an accuracy issue.

options.label: B
options.text: Completeness
options.feedback: Correct. Completeness measures whether all required fields and values are present. A missing required field is a direct completeness failure.

options.label: C
options.text: Consistency
options.feedback: Consistency refers to whether data follows the same format and conventions throughout the dataset. A missing field is not a consistency issue.

options.label: D
options.text: Timeliness
options.feedback: Timeliness refers to whether the data is current enough to be useful. A missing field is not related to when the data was recorded.

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. A missing required field is a completeness failure.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the four data quality dimensions and consider which one specifically addresses whether fields and values are present.

slides.slide_name: True or False — Data Quality Standard Labels
slides.question_body: Determine whether each of the following statements about data quality is True or False.

options.label: A
options.text: A dataset can be accurate but still fail a completeness check.

options.label: B
options.text: Consistency errors occur when data values are factually incorrect.

options.label: C
options.text: Timeliness failures can cause automation to produce valid but outdated outputs.

options.label: D
options.text: Fixing data errors after an automation run is always more efficient than preventing them.

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You evaluated all four data quality statements accurately.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review each dimension independently. Accuracy, completeness, consistency, and timeliness describe different types of data failure.

slides.slide_name: True or False — Data Quality Feedback by Choice
slides.question_body: Select Correct or Incorrect for each statement about data quality best practices.

options.label: A
options.text: Preventive data quality measures are generally more efficient than corrective ones.
options.feedback: Correct. Preventing errors at the point of entry is almost always faster and cheaper than identifying and correcting them after they have propagated through a system.

options.label: B
options.text: Consistency checks compare a value against an external reference database.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Consistency checks compare data values within or across internal datasets to confirm they follow the same format and conventions — not against external databases.

options.label: C
options.text: Required field validation is an example of a preventive data quality measure.
options.feedback: Correct. Required field validation prevents incomplete records from entering the system, stopping a completeness failure before it can occur.

options.label: D
options.text: An outdated record is always inaccurate.
options.feedback: Incorrect. An outdated record may have been accurate when it was recorded. Timeliness and accuracy are separate dimensions — a record can be historically correct but no longer current.

slides.correct_feedback: Well done. You correctly evaluated all four data quality statements.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the distinctions between preventive and corrective measures and between the four data quality dimensions.

slides.slide_name: Matching — Data Quality Dimensions
slides.question_body: Match each data quality dimension to the failure it describes.

options.label: A
options.text: Accuracy
options.match: A contact record contains a phone number that was entered incorrectly

options.label: B
options.text: Completeness
options.match: A course record is missing the required lesson objective field

options.label: C
options.text: Consistency
options.match: The same learner is listed under two different name formats across two systems

options.label: D
options.text: Timeliness
options.match: A pricing file reflects rates from six months ago and is no longer current

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You matched every data quality dimension to the failure it best describes.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Focus on what type of problem each scenario describes — is it wrong, missing, conflicting, or outdated?

slides.slide_name: Sort — Preventive vs Corrective
slides.question_body: Sort each action as either Preventive (stops errors before they occur) or Corrective (fixes errors after they occur).

items.label: A
items.text: Add required field validation to all input forms

items.label: B
items.text: Use dropdown menus to restrict input to approved values

items.label: C
items.text: Run a deduplication script on existing records

items.label: D
items.text: Audit and update outdated records in the system

items.label: E
items.text: Train staff on correct data entry standards before go-live

items.label: F
items.text: Merge duplicate accounts identified during a data review

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You accurately categorized every action as either preventive or corrective.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Think about whether the action stops a problem before it happens or addresses one that already exists.

slides.slide_name: Applying Automation and Data Quality
slides.content:
Putting It All Together

In this final lesson you will apply both automation principles and data quality concepts to real-world scenarios. The activities cover every slide type supported by the importer and include examples of standard feedback, feedback by choice, and custom true/false labels.

As you work through each activity keep these principles in mind:

  • Automation amplifies what is in the source data — quality in, quality out
  • Preventive measures are more efficient than corrective ones
  • Human oversight remains necessary even in fully automated workflows
  • Logs and artifacts are your primary diagnostic tools when something goes wrong

slides.slide_name: Key Concepts Before Final Activities
slides.content:
Key Reminders

Before completing the final activities, review these core takeaways from across the course.

A well-structured process built on clean data and validated outputs is more reliable than any amount of manual effort applied to a poorly structured one.

The goal of automation is not to remove human judgment — it is to apply human judgment less frequently, at the right moments, with better information.

slides.slide_name: Multiple Choice — Applied Scenario Standard Feedback
slides.question_body: An automated content import runs successfully but a reviewer notices that feedback fields are blank on all multiple choice slides. The run log shows no errors. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The automation tool does not support feedback fields on multiple choice slides

options.label: B
options.text: The correct_feedback and incorrect_feedback fields were missing from the source JSON

options.label: C
options.text: The feedback fields require a separate manual entry step after import

options.label: D
options.text: Feedback fields are only supported when feedbackBy is set to choice

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. When the run log shows no errors but fields are blank, the data was missing from the source file. The automation can only populate what exists in the input.
slides.incorrect_feedback: When automation completes without errors but fields are empty, focus on the source data first. The tool writes what the JSON contains — if a field is missing from the JSON it will be blank in the output.

slides.slide_name: Multiple Choice — Applied Scenario Feedback by Choice
slides.question_body: Which combination of conditions produces the most reliable automation output?

options.label: A
options.text: Accurate source data and no post-run validation
options.feedback: Accurate source data is necessary but not sufficient on its own. Skipping post-run validation means errors introduced during the automation process itself would go undetected.

options.label: B
options.text: Accurate, complete, consistent source data combined with post-run spot-checking
options.feedback: Correct. Clean source data across all four quality dimensions combined with post-run validation gives you the highest confidence in automation outputs.

options.label: C
options.text: Fast execution speed and a detailed run log
options.feedback: Speed and logging are valuable but neither guarantees output quality. A fast run of bad data still produces bad outputs, even with a detailed log.

options.label: D
options.text: Manual review of every output record after each run
options.feedback: Manual review of every record defeats the efficiency purpose of automation. Post-run spot-checking is the right balance between oversight and efficiency.

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. Clean source data combined with post-run validation is the most reliable approach.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Think about what it takes both before and after a run to be confident in the outputs.

slides.slide_name: True or False — Applied Standard Labels
slides.question_body: Determine whether each statement is True or False based on the concepts covered in this course.

options.label: A
options.text: A run log that shows zero errors guarantees that all output fields were populated correctly.

options.label: B
options.text: Automation can resume from a specific lesson without reprocessing previously completed slides.

options.label: C
options.text: Correcting data errors after an automated run is always more efficient than preventing them.

options.label: D
options.text: Failure artifacts such as screenshots help diagnose what went wrong during an automated run.

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You evaluated all four statements accurately.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the principles covered across all three lessons and consider the relationship between logs, data quality, and reliable outputs.

slides.slide_name: True or False — Applied Feedback by Choice Custom Labels
slides.question_body: Select Supported or Not Supported for each feature based on what the LEAP Importer tool handles automatically.

options.label: A
options.text: Creating lesson titles inside LEAP before an import runs.
options.feedback: Not supported by the tool. Lesson titles must be created manually in LEAP before running an import. The tool creates slides inside existing lessons — it does not create the lessons themselves.

options.label: B
options.text: Automatically skipping slides that were already created in a previous run.
options.feedback: Supported. In Normal mode the tool reads the persistent run log and skips any slide that was already completed successfully in a previous run.

options.label: C
options.text: Capturing a screenshot when a slide fails during an import.
options.feedback: Supported. When a slide fails the tool automatically captures a full-page screenshot and saves it to the run output folder for diagnostic review.

options.label: D
options.text: Automatically deleting existing slides before recreating them in Rebuild mode.
options.feedback: Not supported. Rebuild mode recreates slides from scratch but does not delete existing ones first. Running Rebuild on a lesson that already has slides may produce duplicates.

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You accurately identified what the tool supports and what requires manual steps.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the tool capabilities covered in the user guide, particularly the differences between Normal and Rebuild modes.

slides.slide_name: Matching — Concepts to Scenarios
slides.question_body: Match each scenario to the concept it best illustrates.

options.label: A
options.text: An import runs with no errors but feedback fields are blank on every slide
options.match: Source data was missing required fields

options.label: B
options.text: A second run skips all slides from the first run and only creates new ones
options.match: Normal mode using the persistent run log

options.label: C
options.text: A screenshot is saved showing a validation error in LEAP at the point of failure
options.match: Failure artifact captured during a run

options.label: D
options.text: All slides are recreated from scratch regardless of prior run history
options.match: Rebuild mode ignoring the run log

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You matched every scenario to its corresponding automation concept.
slides.incorrect_feedback: Review the tool behavior covered in the user guide for each scenario.

items.label: B

items.label: C

items.label: D

items.label: E

slides.correct_feedback: Correct. You sorted every step into the right phase of the import workflow.
